papers.title: Think2Listen: Evidence-Centric Learning For Agentic Audio Understanding With LALMS
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large audio-language models (LALMs) have broadened audio understanding across speech, sound, and music, with tool-based agents further supporting these tasks by invoking predefined audio tools. However, a persistent gap remains between perceiving acoustic content and using it as evidence for reasoning: recognizing what is audible does not ensure that a model can identify which cues resolve an uncertain decision. To bridge this gap, we propose Think2Listen, an evidence-centric learning framework for agentic audio understanding. Guided by evidence before commitment, Think2Listen couples iterative reasoning with a targeted LALM interaction to actively seek acoustic cues that distinguish competing hypotheses and revise candidate judgments based on the observations returned. It learns what to ask, how to use evidence, and when to stop, using observation-induced changes in candidate-state to inform training credit. Extensive evaluations on two benchmarks spanning seven audio categories demonstrate that Think2Listen achieves (I) enhanced multi-step audio reasoning, with gains in overall accuracy of 5.08%--17.67% over competing audio agents; and (II) improved audio understanding and reasoning across speech, sound, and music, boosting overall accuracy by 2.29%--13.10% over the corresponding baselines. The source code is available at https://github.com/JinWang79/Think2Listen.
reasons: Audio Understanding & Reasoning: audio reasoning, audio understanding
Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model

papers.title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing. To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio large language model, audio llm

papers.title: Progressive Layer-wise Supervision: Deep-to-Shallow Supervision Annealing for Efficient and Robust Speech Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Speech foundation models pretrained via self-supervised learning provide powerful representations for deepfake detection, yet we find that standard fine-tuning exploits only the deepest transformer layers-leaving the majority of the network's capacity discriminatively inert. Layer-wise probing of XLS-R-128 reveals that the top two-thirds of the transformer stack contribute negligibly to anti-spoofing performance after standard fine-tuning, a phenomenon we term shallow-layer dormancy. We connect this observation to the representational redundancy of pretrained transformers: adjacent layers encode highly similar information, and fine-tuning without explicit intermediate supervision reinforces rather than breaks this redundancy. To address this, we propose Progressive Layer-wise Supervision (PLS), a training framework that attaches a shared linear classifier to every transformer layer and schedules layer-wise loss contributions via an exponentially annealed power weighting. Early training concentrates supervision on deep layers to preserve the pretrained representational hierarchy; later training progressively redistributes supervision to shallower layers, converting dormant earlier representations into discriminative ones. Competitive detection (<9.25% average EER) is achievable on XLS-R-128 at layer 7, which reduces the parameter count from 315M to 101M and exemplifies an early exit mechanism. Experiments across twelve benchmarks spanning in-domain, and out-of-domain deepfake scenarios show PLS achieves a new state-of-the-art with 239M parameters, outperforming prior methods with larger and more complex architectures.

Audio & Speech Language Models: speech foundation model

papers.title: Rethinking Post-Training for Expressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Zero-shot voice cloning typically emphasizes preserving the timbre and prosodic characteristics of a reference speaker. However, in real-world use, speech should adapt its delivery to the target text rather than remain tied to a fixed speaking style. In this work, we formulate this problem as text-adaptive prosody synthesis for zero-shot voice cloning and study how post-training can endow a cloning model with this capability. We develop a three-stage framework. First, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a cold start by aligning the model with text-appropriate expressive speech. Second, Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) jointly optimizes prosodic expressiveness, acoustic quality, intelligibility, and speaker similarity. Finally, context-conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) enables self-improvement by transferring expressive behavior from strong-reference to weak-reference conditions. On Qwen3-TTS, our framework improves Emotion from 18.5 to 81.2 and Paralinguistics from 38.4 to 73.9. Extensive ablations validate the role of each stage.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech, voice cloning

papers.title: Learning from Distribution: Rethinking One-Hot Supervision for ASR and QA in Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Speech language models (SLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and general-purpose speech understanding, yet ASR-specific training often degrades spoken question answering (QA) performance. We revisit this conflict from the perspective of task-specific input--output mappings and one-hot supervision. Our findings reveal pronounced task-asymmetric effects: ASR-only training severely limits QA capability, whereas QA-only training retains reasonable ASR performance. We hypothesize that the relatively deterministic mapping of ASR, combined with single-reference supervision, biases models toward transcription-specific behavior. Motivated by this perspective, we advocate broadening ASR learning objectives while preserving recognition accuracy. We propose Learning from Distribution (LFD), which aligns speech-conditioned predictions with the conditional output distributions of a pretrained text LLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFD improves both ASR and QA performance, exhibits superior data efficiency, and remains effective under full-parameter fine-tuning. CoT-ASR further supports the broader applicability of our proposed supervision principle.

Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: automatic speech recognition

papers.title: Factorized Self-Supervised Speech Tokenization
papers.abstract: Speech tokenizers convert audio into discrete units, enabling language models to process and generate speech. The goal is to learn compact, text-like representations while preserving enough detail to reconstruct a speaker's voice and delivery. We propose Facto: a factorized tokenizer that disentangles time-varying information (content and prosody) from static components (speaker identity and recording conditions). We build on a recent linear factorization method for self-supervised features, extending it to handle unseen speakers. Then, we cluster the factorized space and train a lightweight decoder to reconstruct audio from the resulting tokens. By removing the static components before clustering, our tokens are more robust to small noise perturbations. We validate this by testing token stability under various noise conditions. Next, we theoretically analyze Facto's convergence and scaling properties, quantifying how the factorization improves with the number of training speakers. Finally, we evaluate Facto on a range of downstream tasks. We show that greater token stability translates into improved text-to-speech performance and competitive results in voice conversion and spoken language modeling. Code and checkpoints at https://github.com/ubisoft/ubisoft-laforge-facto/ and demo page at https://ubisoft-laforge.github.io/speech/facto/.

papers.title: Beyond Controllability: Speaker Diversity in Instruction-Guided Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Instruction-guided text-to-speech (ITTS) lets users specify voice properties in natural language. Applications from conversational AI character voices to synthetic training data for downstream speech models depend on the system producing many distinct voices when the same broad category is requested repeatedly. No prior work audits whether ITTS outputs are in fact diverse, either compared to real speech or across attribute values. We evaluate seven open-source ITTS systems using speaker embeddings whose representational capacity we independently validate. Every system produces speaker distributions markedly narrower than real speech. Furthermore, female prompts produce less diverse voice pools than male prompts across most systems. In contrast, accent and emotion prompts barely alter speaker diversity in most systems, but reveal a strong controllability bias toward North American English and neutral speech. These results show that diversity and controllability capture complementary weaknesses, neither of which alone is sufficient to evaluate ITTS. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/dlion168/ITTS-Speaker-Diversity.

papers.title: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery
papers.abstract: Natural speech conveys meaning not only through words, but also through the prominence on a few words. Yet most text-to-speech (TTS) systems remain prominence-unaware, existing prominence-aware TTS require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate in isolation, disconnected from synthesis. This creates a fundamental gap no existing system can automatically discover where stress should be placed, realize it as natural-sounding prosody, and offer user control over emphasis placement, all within a single model. To circumvent this, we propose ProTTS, a unified framework where stress detection emerges from the TTS model itself and, in turn, guides it to synthesize more natural and controllable speech. We incorporate a clustering head into the variance adaptor of FastSpeech_2 that discovers word stress directly from aggregated prosodic features. The discovered stress then drives emphasis variance predictors that modify pitch, energy, and duration for stressed words. The framework is trained end-to-end: TTS reconstruction and clustering losses jointly shape a stress-discriminative feature space without requiring stress labels at any stage. At inference, the same architecture also supports user-controllable emphasis by accepting a custom stress mask. We evaluate ProTTS on ISLE (non-native), LibriTTS, VCTK (native training), and three evaluation benchmarks (Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, EmphAssess). Listeners prefer ProTTS over the baseline with a MOS of 3.96 vs. 3.12 and 83.5% preference rate. For stress detection, ProTTS achieves 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (German/Italian L2), outperforming unsupervised (0.70) and supervised (0.82) baselines, and 0.933 F1 in zero-shot transfer to Tatoeba.

papers.title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Token Transfer for Data-Efficient Non-Verbal Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and breath, carry affective cues that words alone do not convey. Yet NV data remains scarce because speech annotation pipelines often omit or normalize these events. Existing work has improved NV text-to-speech through model design and data curation, but whether one NV token can help a model learn another has received little systematic study. We investigate this cross-token transferability in a controlled CosyVoice 2 setup. We first trace a laughter-only scaling curve, then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech. With only 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises end-to-end laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing the 0.495 obtained from 1,600 laughter examples alone. At the 1,600-example anchor, cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697). Waveform-level Whisper-D scoring and a semantic-token transcriber show consistent trends. Cross-token transfer therefore offers a complementary route to low-resource NV generation.

No-Shot Text-to-Speech: Limitations of Zero-Shot TTS and its Evaluation Methods in Representing Queer and Transgender Voices
papers.abstract: Gender expansive voices remain underrepresented in speech datasets, which could cause challenges with generalizability in zero-shot Text-To-Speech (TTS) systems. We evaluate six zero-shot TTS models on two datasets: one containing non gender expansive voices (N-GE) and one with gender expansive (GE) voices from self-identified speakers. Human ratings found that 2 of the 6 models synthesize less similar GE voices compared to N-GE voices, and 3 have improved performance for GE voices. Automated evaluations yield conflicting results, with speaker similarity and automated mean opinion score predictors rating performance of GE voices inconsistently between models and human ratings. This highlights a potential blind spot in evaluation pipelines, emphasizing a need for more representative data and metrics that better capture human perceptual judgments. Our findings stress the need to include transgender, queer, and minority communities in creation of better datasets and model training.

papers.title: Auditory-Feedback-Conditioned Flow TTS for Implicit Lombard Adaptation
papers.abstract: Conventional text-to-speech (TTS) systems can lose intelligibility in noise environments because they cannot adapt to environmental changes. However, humans tend to increase their vocal efforts in noisy environments, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. Building on an auditory-feedback Lombard TTS, we investigate whether a pretrained Flow-based TTS can learn acoustic adaptation directly from auditory feedback without explicit prosodic control. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feedback and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback are extracted from the noise-corrupted waveforms and injected into the Flow-matching condition for utterance refinement and causal block-level updates. We assess feedback benefits across prompting and noise conditions using plain/Lombard prompting, prompt-switching controls, and paired-finetuning. Experiments show that while finetuning provides strong robustness under in-domain conditions, auditory feedback yields additional cue-dependent benefits that generalize to unseen noise. Moreover, stronger power/F0 tracking alone does not guarantee better speech intelligibility or quality.

papers.title: A Speech-LLM Framework for Enrollment-Free Wake-Word-Guided Target-Speaker Recognition in Complex Noisy Scenarios for Seamless Human-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: Target-speaker automatic speech recognition (TS-ASR) is essential for reliable human-machine interaction in complex acoustic environments, where overlapping speech and background noise make it difficult to identify and recognize the intended speaker. Existing approaches typically rely on speaker enrollment or cascaded processing pipelines, limiting their flexibility in practical applications. To address these limitations, we propose an enrollment-free Speech-LLM framework that leverages wake-word text as a lexical cue to guide target-speaker recognition. Specifically, a text-cue encoder extracts lexical representations from the wake word, which are integrated into a pretrained speech encoder through cross-attention to establish an implicit association between the wake-word occurrence and the target speaker. This enables the model to selectively recognize subsequent commands from the target speaker without requiring enrollment speech or explicit wake-word boundaries. Furthermore, a large language model (LLM) unifies command transcription and non-target speaker rejection within a single autoregressive framework. To improve robustness against complex acoustic interference, we develop a large-scale speech synthesis and simulation pipeline with a progressive four-stage training strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a command character error rate of 16.15% and a non-target speaker rejection rate of 91.56%, yielding a unified score of 87.70%, compared with 71.70% for the strongest enrollment-free baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of wake-word-guided speaker selection and highlight the potential of integrating target-speaker recognition and rejection within a unified Speech-LLM framework for robust human-machine interaction.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech synthesis, automatic speech recognition

papers.title: Real-Time French Speech Translation into Four Congolese National Languages Using Whisper and Language-Specific LoRA Adapters for NLLB-200
papers.abstract: French is the sole official language of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, yet much of the population communicates daily in Lingala, Swahili, Tshiluba or Kikongo. This paper presents a cascaded system that transcribes spoken French with Whisper and translates it with NLLB-200-distilled-600M, specialized by one Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter per target language on a shared frozen base model.
papers.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology

papers.title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
papers.abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

papers.title: Post-fusion Event-aware Time-Frequency Refinement for Audio Moment Retrieval
papers.abstract: Audio Moment Retrieval (AMR) aims to locate the temporal segment within a long audio recording that semantically corresponds to a natural-language query. This task is particularly challenging because query-related audio events are often sparsely distributed and embedded in complex acoustic environments, where background sounds and acoustically similar events can easily obscure the target moments. Existing methods mainly strengthen audio-text semantic interaction to enhance the query-related information in audio frames, but seldom refine the resulting audio representations before temporal localization, limiting their ability to accurately distinguish target events from irrelevant acoustic interference. To address this issue, we propose ETR-AMR, a post-fusion event-aware time-frequency refinement framework for AMR. Specifically, an event-aware time-frequency refinement (ETR) strategy is proposed after audio-text interaction to refine fused audio frame features before temporal moment localization. ETR consists of two complementary mechanisms: time frame gating and frequency refinement. The time frame gating mechanism estimates frame-wise event relevance to emphasize query-related audio frames and suppress redundant temporal responses, while frequency refinement applies learnable time-frequency reweighting to enhance discriminative event-related frequency patterns and reduce background-dominant interference. By jointly refining fused audio frame features in the temporal and frequency domains, ETR produces more discriminative event-aware features for accurate temporal boundary prediction. Experiments on four AMR datasets demonstrate that ETR-AMR achieves superior performance compared with existing methods, especially on the high-quality CASTELLA benchmark. Duration-wise analysis further confirms the effectiveness of ETR for medium and long audio moments.

papers.title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
papers.abstract: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

papers.title: Where Is Rank-1 DiM Refusal Intervenable in Multimodal LM Derivatives?
papers.abstract: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

# MiniMax Music 3 **MiniMax Music 3** is a high-performance music generation model for creating complete songs up to **five minutes** long. Conditioned on lyrics and a detailed music description, it generates structurally coherent songs with expressive vocals, evolving arrangements, and stable long-form audio quality. MiniMax Music 3 combines an **8B Global LLM** for long-range musical structure, a **0.6B Local LLM** for frame-level acoustic detail, and a continuous hidden-state synthesis system based on **Flow Matching** and **Flow-VAE**. The model produces 32 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV audio. ## Demo Explore music generation examples on the [MiniMax Music 3 Demo](https://minimax-ai.github.io/music3-demo/).

## Complete Songs with Long-Range Coherence MiniMax Music 3 natively supports full-song generation up to five minutes. The model maintains musical themes, rhythm, vocal identity, and arrangement progression across long sequences, enabling complete structures such as intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, instrumental break, and outro. ## Fine-Grained Music Control The model accepts two complementary inputs: - **Lyrics** define the words to be sung and may include explicit section tags such as `[Intro]`, `[Verse]`, `[Pre-Chorus]`, `[Chorus]`, `[Post-Chorus]`, `[Bridge]`, `[Instrumental]`, `[Solo]`, and `[Outro]`. - **Music description** defines the musical style, emotional progression, vocal performance, instrumentation, arrangement, and production profile. For precise control, we recommend using a Structured Caption with three sections: - **Global Metadata**: genre, subgenre, BPM, key, scale, emotional progression, listening scenario, and production profile. - **Vocal Details**: vocal gender, timbre, performance style, harmony, backing vocals, and vocal effects. - **Arrangement**: primary and secondary instruments, section-level instrument evolution, groove, bass, percussion, textures, and spatial effects. This representation allows the model to follow not only a global style, but also the musical development of the song over time. ## Hybrid-LM MiniMax Music 3 uses a hierarchical autoregressive architecture that separates global musical modeling from local acoustic modeling. - The **Global LLM (8B)** predicts the first RVQ codebook frame by frame and models the song's long-range semantic and structural progression. - The **Local LLM (0.6B)** predicts the remaining acoustic codebooks within each frame and restores fine-grained acoustic information. The Global LLM is initialized from Qwen3-8B. During training, its embedding and output layers are first adapted to semantic music tokens. The Global and Local LLMs are then jointly trained to model all RVQ codebooks. ## Continuous Hidden-State Synthesis Instead of decoding only from discrete RVQ tokens, the synthesis module fuses the final hidden states of the Global and Local LLMs. These continuous representations preserve richer acoustic information for vocal articulation, instrumental texture, and temporal continuity. The synthesis path is: ```text Global and Local LLM hidden states ↓ Hidden-state fusion ↓ Flow Matching (2.4B) ↓ Flow-VAE latent ↓ Flow-VAE Decoder (123M) ↓ 32 kHz stereo audio ``` The Flow-VAE architecture is adapted from MiniMax Speech and retrained for the dynamic range and spectral characteristics of music. ## Music Tokenizer The training tokenizer uses eight layers of Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ): - The first semantic codebook contains **16,384** entries and captures the core musical semantics and structure. - The remaining seven acoustic codebooks contain **1,024** entries each and represent residual acoustic details. Training first optimizes the semantic codebook, then jointly trains all eight codebooks. At inference time, waveform synthesis uses the fused LLM hidden states and does not require the discrete tokenizer decoder. ## How to Use MiniMax Music 3 is supported by [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni). Follow the official [installation guide](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/get_started/installation.html) to prepare the runtime environment. ### Download the Model ```bash hf download MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3 --local-dir /path/to/minimax_ttm ``` We recommend the following inference frameworks to serve the model: - [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/) \- see [cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/minimax_music3.html) - [diffusers](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers) \- see [diffusers docs](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/minimax-music3-integration/docs/source/en/api/pipelines/minimax_music3.md) - [ComfyUI](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI) see [comfyUI tutorials](https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/audio/minimax/minimax-music-3) ### Serve with SGLang-Omni ```bash sgl-omni serve --model-path MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3 --port 8000 ``` ### Generate Music The service uses the shared speech API. Put the lyrics in `input` and the music description in `instructions`. Put lyric structure tags such as `[Verse]` and `[Chorus]` on their own lines. ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/audio/speech \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3", "input": "[Verse]\nMorning light filtering through the pine\n[Chorus]\nSoftly the world begins to breathe", "instructions": "A warm acoustic pop song with intimate female vocals, fingerpicked guitar, soft piano, and a gradual emotional build into a wide final chorus.", "response_format": "wav", "seed": 7, "max_new_tokens": 750, "stream": false }' \ --output minimax_music3.wav ``` `max_new_tokens` sets the maximum number of audio frames at 25 frames per second. Generation may finish before this limit when the model emits an end-of-audio token. The response is a 32 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV file. ### Reproducible Example The following end-to-end example contains the complete lyrics, music description, and generation parameters used to produce the reference audio. | Use case | Request | Result | |---|---|---| | Text-to-music | [View script](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3/blob/main/scripts/end_to_end/minimax_ttm_test.py) | [minimax_ttm.wav](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3/blob/main/assets/minimax_ttm.wav) | ## 🧨 Diffusers MiniMax Music 3 is available as a [diffusers](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers) modular pipeline. Until [huggingface/diffusers#14456](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/pull/14456) is merged, install diffusers from the PR commit: The snippet below fits 24GB+ VRAM GPUs ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers@dafe3733fcfdbf3c48915fe77be3aef65b5d6a2d transformers accelerate soundfile ``` ```python import soundfile as sf import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3") pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) pipe.to("cuda") lyrics = """[verse] Morning light filtering through the pine Every quiet street is yours and mine [chorus] Softly the world begins to breathe""" prompt = ( "Genre: acoustic pop. BPM: 96. Key: C major. Warm and intimate, building gently into the chorus. " "Vocals: soft female lead, close and breathy, light stacked harmonies in the chorus. " "Arrangement: fingerpicked guitar and soft piano; brushed drums and upright bass enter in the chorus." ) audio = pipe( prompt=prompt, lyrics=lyrics, audio_duration=60.0, generator=torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(7), output="audios", )[0] sf.write("song.wav", audio.T.float().cpu().numpy(), pipe.sampling_rate) ``` ### Low VRAM The full precision fits under 24GB of VRAM. With automatic CPU offloading, generation takes in ~22 GB; additionally streaming the language model layer by layer makes it fit even 8 GB video cards: ```python import torch from diffusers import ComponentsManager, ModularPipeline from diffusers.hooks import apply_group_offloading manager = ComponentsManager() manager.enable_auto_cpu_offload(device="cuda") pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3", components_manager=manager) pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) # Only needed below ~22 GB of VRAM — slower, but fits in 8 GB. apply_group_offloading( pipe.language_model, onload_device=torch.device("cuda"), offload_type="leaf_level", use_stream=True ) ``` ## Prompt Enhancement A concise natural-language description can be used directly. For richer prompts and more precise control, use the provided [`music-caption-rewriter`](https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-Music3/tree/main/skills/music-caption-rewriter) skill to expand it into a Structured Caption containing `Global Metadata`, `Vocal Details`, and `Arrangement`. The skill preserves musical instructions attached to lyric section tags in the arrangement description while keeping the lyric text in the lyrics input. ```bash npx skills add MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-Music3 --skill music-caption-rewriter ``` ## Limitations - Inference requires CUDA. - Only non-streaming generation is currently supported. - The tokenized text prompt is limited to 5,000 tokens. - Audio generation is limited to 9,000 acoustic frames. - Section tags and music descriptions provide generative control rather than strict symbolic guarantees. The generated tempo, key, instrumentation, lyrics, and song structure may not always match every requested detail exactly. ## Contact Us Contact us at [model@minimax.io](mailto:model@minimax.io).

# **MiniMax-Music3-GGUF**

> **MiniMax Music 3** is an open-weights text-to-music generation model from MiniMax AI that creates complete, structurally coherent songs up to five minutes long in 32 kHz, 16-bit stereo WAV format. Conditioned on section-tagged lyrics (such as `[Verse]` and `[Chorus]`) and detailed style descriptions covering metadata, vocals, and arrangement, it uses a hierarchical Hybrid-LM architecture pairing a Qwen3-initialized **8B Global LLM** for long-range musical structure with a **0.6B Local LLM** for frame-level acoustic detail. Instead of decoding directly from discrete Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) tokens, the system fuses the hidden states of both language models and synthesizes high-fidelity audio through a **2.4B Flow Matching** module and **Flow-VAE** decoder, supporting deployment via SGLang-Omni, Hugging Face `diffusers`, and ComfyUI—even scaling down to 8 GB VRAM GPUs with layer offloading.

# ACE-Step 1.5 — Qwen3.5-0.8B 5Hz Planner (GGUF)

Experimental **GGUF** release (`Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF`) of a **Qwen3.5-0.8B** (`18 GatedDeltaNet + 6 full-attention` layers, `V = 313,612` extended vocabulary with 64,000 5Hz audio code tokens) semantic-audio planner for **ACE-Step 1.5**.

- **Companion All-in-One Apple Silicon MLX Repository:** [`Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX`](https://huggingface.co/Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX)
- **Out-of-the-Box Single-Command Workflow:** `generate.py` runs the `qwen35` GGUF composer via `llama-cpp-python` (with constrained 6-field YAML CoT + CFG Stage-2 audio-code logits processors and default anti-repeat post-processing matching the MLX implementation) and pairs it with the official Python **ACE-Step 1.5** DiT/VAE renderer. On first run, `generate.py` automatically downloads only the required official renderer files (`acestep-v15-turbo`, `vae`, `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`) from [`ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5`](https://huggingface.co/ACE-Step/Ace-Step1.5) (pinned revision `19671f406d603126926c1b7e2adc169acbcade22`) into your standard Hugging Face cache (`HF_HOME`), after which generation works completely offline (`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`).

> **Important Status Notice:**
> 1. **`ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-BF16.gguf` is the primary model.** `ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf` is provided **solely as a lower-memory deployment option (not the primary result)**. Lower-bit quantizations (`Q4_*`, `Q5_*`, `Q6_K`) are intentionally omitted because sub-8-bit quantization degrades discrete 5Hz semantic audio code generation.
> 2. **Honest Benchmark Summary:** This is an **experimental research checkpoint** (`S-lr3e5-best-bf16`, step `975`, Epoch `3`) selected strictly by lowest validation masked cross-entropy (`6.933546922`). On raw `dev-100` decoding, **the official `ACE-Step/acestep-5Hz-lm-0.6B` baseline is faster (`5.71 s` vs. `7.96 s`), achieves higher strict validity (`100/100` vs. `97/100`), and scores higher on CLAP (`0.3451` vs. `0.2832` / `0.2920`)**. Overall quality evaluation remains **`INCOMPLETE`**. Because the raw 0.8B student exhibits lower audio-code diversity (`0.4326` mean unique ratio) and can collapse into late-sequence short or single-code loops on longer tracks, `generate.py` **enables inference-time anti-repeat post-processing by default** (disable via `--no-antirepeat`). See [Anti-Repeat Decoding (Default On)](#anti-repeat-decoding-default-on), [Evaluation (`dev-100`)](#evaluation-dev-100), and [Limitations](#limitations) before use.

This 40-second sample was generated with the companion [MLX package](https://huggingface.co/Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX) Qwen3.5-0.8B composer and the official ACE-Step 1.5 DiT/VAE (same weights; the GGUF files in this repository are a conversion). `generate.py` defaults, anti-repeat on, seed `42`. <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF/resolve/main/samples/demo_40s.mp3"></audio>

**Live radio:** [ACE Radio on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r4C8z3VA3fQ), a live stream of songs generated on the fly by the companion [MLX package](https://huggingface.co/Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX) Qwen3.5-0.8B composer with the ACE-Step 1.5 DiT/VAE.

## Included GGUF Files

| File | Role | Quantization | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| `ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-BF16.gguf` | **Primary Model** (`--quant bf16`, default) | `BF16` (`F32` GDN recurrent/norm tensors) | `1.54 GiB` (`1,652,539,360` B) | Lossless conversion of winner `S-lr3e5-best-bf16`; `100%` (`64/64`) top-1 parity with MLX `bf16` |

Both GGUF files embed the full `313,612`-token `qwen35` BPE + `<|audio_code_0..63999|>` vocabulary (`llama.cpp` `b9810`+ compatible).

## Quickstart (Fresh Virtual Environment)

Requires **Python 3.12** (`>=3.11,<3.13`) and a C/C++ toolchain (`cmake`) if `llama-cpp-python==0.3.37` builds from source. On **Apple Silicon Macs (`arm64`)**, enable Metal acceleration via `CMAKE_ARGS="-DGGML_METAL=on"`:

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
CMAKE_ARGS="-DGGML_METAL=on" pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### One-Line Generation Examples

Generate a 30-second English vocal track with the **primary `BF16` GGUF** (anti-repeat enabled by default; first run downloads ~6.3 GB of official ACE-Step 1.5 renderer weights to `HF_HOME`, and subsequent runs work offline):

```bash
python generate.py --prompt "upbeat indie synth-pop, pulsing analog bass, crisp drums, bright synth hooks, warm female vocals" --lyrics "[Verse 1]\nMorning light across the avenue\nEvery shadow turns to gold with you\n[Chorus]\nRun into the open sky tonight\nChasing echoes in the neon light" --duration 30 --out vocal_30s.wav
```

Generate using the **`Q8_0` deployment option**:

```bash
python generate.py --quant q8_0 --prompt "upbeat indie synth-pop, pulsing analog bass, crisp drums, bright synth hooks, warm female vocals" --lyrics "[Verse 1]\nMorning light across the avenue\nEvery shadow turns to gold with you\n[Chorus]\nRun into the open sky tonight\nChasing echoes in the neon light" --duration 30 --out vocal_30s_q8.wav
```

Run completely offline once the official renderer has been cached in `HF_HOME`:

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python generate.py --prompt "cinematic acoustic guitar and warm strings, gentle fingerpicking, peaceful autumn atmosphere, instrumental" --lyrics "[Instrumental]" --duration 30 --out instrumental_30s.wav
```

Disable anti-repeat post-processing to reproduce exact raw model decoding (bit-identical audio codes to the unpenalized GGUF planner for the same quantization, seed, and parameters):

```bash
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 python generate.py --no-antirepeat --quant q8_0 --prompt "cinematic acoustic guitar and warm strings, gentle fingerpicking, peaceful autumn atmosphere, instrumental" --lyrics "[Instrumental]" --duration 30 --seed 42 --out instrumental_raw_30s.wav
```

---

## Anti-Repeat Decoding (Default On)

In raw Stage-2 sampling, this distilled 0.8B planner can occasionally fall into repetitive short cycles or single-code stutters on longer durations (e.g., `60–120 s`). `generate.py` therefore enables an **inference-time anti-repeat post-processing and quality-gate pipeline by default** during Stage-2 5Hz audio-code generation (`Stage-1` `<think>...</think>` YAML CoT decoding is unchanged, matching [`Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX`](https://huggingface.co/Jakevin/ACE-Step1.5-Qwen3.5-0.8B-MLX)).

### Stage-2 Per-Step Sampling Order

At each Stage-2 audio-code step (`step_i` in `0 .. 5 * duration - 1`), `generate.py` extracts `float32` logits from `llama.cpp` (`llama_get_logits_ith`) and applies operations in strict order:

1. **CFG Merge:** `step_logits = uncond + cfg_scale * (cond - uncond)` (when `--cfg-scale > 1.0`).
2. **Audio-Code Vocabulary Mask:** Restrict valid tokens strictly to `<|audio_code_0|> .. <|audio_code_63999|>` (`-1e9` outside the 64,000 audio codes; `<|im_end|>` forced once `5 * duration` codes are emitted).
3. **Windowed Penalties, N-Gram Blocking & Late Temperature Schedule:**
   - **Windowed Repetition / Frequency / Presence Penalties** over the **last `40` generated codes** (`8.0 s` at `5 Hz`): multiplicative/divisive repetition penalty `1.2`, additive frequency penalty `0.25 * count`, and flat presence penalty `0.15`.
   - **Windowed 8-Gram Blocking** over the **last `80` generated codes** (`16.0 s` at `5 Hz`): forbids repeating any `8`-gram (`1.6 s` span; `max_count = 1`, setting the completion logit to `-1e9`).
   - **Late-Sequence Linear Temperature Ramp:** holds `--temperature` (`0.85`) through the first `40%` of audio-code steps, then linearly increases effective temperature from `0.85` to `1.05` (`--temperature-late`) over the remaining `60%` of the sequence.
4. **Softmax & Top-p Nucleus Sampling:** `float64` softmax followed by nucleus sampling (`--top-p 0.9`) driven by `np.random.Generator(PCG64(seed))`.

### Quality Gate & Definition of "Best" Attempt

After generating the full sequence of `5 * duration` audio codes, `generate.py` evaluates three repetition quality-gate thresholds:

- **Overall Unique Code Ratio:** `unique_code_ratio >= 0.58`
- **Second-Half 8-Gram Repeat Rate:** `late_ngram_repeat_ratio <= 0.50` (fraction of `8`-grams in the second half of the track that already appeared in the first half)
- **Longest Contiguous Periodic Cycle:** `longest_cycle_frac <= 0.30` (longest immediately repeating cycle of period `1..64` codes divided by total code count)

If an attempt fails any of these three thresholds, `generate.py` re-runs the planner with a deterministic stepped seed (`seed + 100 * regen_index`) for **at most `--max-regen 3` total attempts** (`seed`, `seed + 100`, `seed + 200`), stopping immediately on the first attempt that passes all three thresholds.

**How the "best" attempt is selected:**
1. Any valid attempt that passes all three quality-gate thresholds (`passed_thresholds = true`) takes priority over attempts that do not, and terminates the retry loop immediately.
2. If all `--max-regen` attempts fail at least one threshold, `generate.py` keeps the valid attempt with the highest composite **`quality_score`**:

```text
quality_score = unique_code_ratio
              + 0.25 * late_unique_code_ratio
              + 0.25 * ngram8_unique_ratio
              - 0.60 * late_ngram_repeat_ratio
              - 0.60 * longest_cycle_frac
```

When `--save-meta-json <path>` is supplied (and in the JSON summary printed to `stdout`), `generate.py` records `repetition_metrics`, `quality_score`, `passed_thresholds`, `regen_attempts` (with each attempt's `seed`, `passed_thresholds`, `metrics`, and `quality_score`), and the full `audio_codes` integer array.

### CLI Anti-Repeat Flags & Defaults

| CLI Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| `--no-antirepeat` (`--antirepeat-off`) | `False` (enabled) | Disable all anti-repeat penalties, temperature ramp, and quality-gate retries; produces identical audio codes to original raw `generate.py` |
| `--repetition-penalty` | `1.2` | Multiplicative/divisive repetition penalty within `--penalty-window` (`1.0` disables) |
| `--frequency-penalty` | `0.25` | Additive penalty per code occurrence within `--penalty-window` (`0.0` disables) |
| `--presence-penalty` | `0.15` | Flat additive penalty for any code present within `--penalty-window` (`0.0` disables) |
| `--penalty-window` | `40` | Lookback window in audio codes (`40` codes = `8.0 s` at `5 Hz`; `0` = full history) |
| `--no-repeat-ngram` | `8` | N-gram size blocked from repeating within `--no-repeat-ngram-window` (`0` disables) |
| `--no-repeat-ngram-window` | `80` | Lookback window in audio codes for n-gram blocking (`80` codes = `16.0 s` at `5 Hz`; `0` = full history) |
| `--no-repeat-ngram-max-count` | `1` | Max occurrences of an n-gram allowed in the window before masking to `-1e9` (`1` = forbid repeats) |
| `--temperature` | `0.85` | Base planner temperature (Stage-1 CoT and first `40%` of Stage-2 audio codes) |
| `--temperature-late` | `1.05` | Target temperature at the end of Stage-2 generation (set equal to `--temperature` to disable ramp) |
| `--temperature-late-start-frac` | `0.40` | Generation progress fraction (`0.40` = `40%`) where the linear temperature ramp starts |
| `--unique-code-ratio-min` | `0.58` | Quality-gate minimum overall unique audio-code ratio |
| `--late-ngram-size` | `8` | N-gram size used for `late_ngram_repeat_ratio` |
| `--late-ngram-repeat-max` | `0.50` | Quality-gate maximum second-half n-gram repeat ratio |
| `--longest-cycle-frac-max` | `0.30` | Quality-gate maximum fraction of codes covered by a contiguous periodic loop |
| `--max-regen` | `3` | Maximum total planner attempts across stepped seeds (`seed`, `seed+100`, `seed+200`) |
| `--save-meta-json` | `None` | Save full run metadata JSON (including `repetition_metrics`, `regen_attempts`, and `audio_codes`) |
| `--save-codes-json` | `None` | Optional path to save `{audio_codes, audio_codes_str, n_codes}` as a standalone JSON |
| `--skip-render` | `False` | Run Stage-A GGUF planner only without loading or downloading DiT/VAE |

## Evaluation (`dev-100`)

> **Important Note on `dev-100` Scores vs. Default Anti-Repeat:** All `dev-100` evaluation results in the tables below are **raw model decoding outputs WITHOUT anti-repeat enabled** (equivalent to `--no-antirepeat`, `max_retries = 0`). The anti-repeat penalties, late temperature ramp, and quality-gate regeneration in `generate.py` are **inference-time post-processing heuristics** and **have NOT been formally re-evaluated on the same `dev-100` benchmark**.

All metrics below are from the pre-registered single-shot constrained `dev-100` evaluation of the underlying `bf16` checkpoint (`50` English CC0 vocal prompts + `50` `[Instrumental]` prompts across `30–120 s`, `max_retries = 0`, Stream-A constrained decoding with `temperature = 0.85`, `top_p = 0.9`, `cfg_scale = 2.0`, no anti-repeat penalties, and 8-step `acestep-v15-turbo` `strict_planner` rendering on an Apple M4 Pro with `64 GB` RAM).

`S-lr3e5-best-bf16` was selected solely by the frozen CE-first rule (`-0.022018514` lower masked CE vs. the `lr = 1e-4` student). Lower validation CE **did not** translate into superior downstream audio metrics.

### Downstream Audio & Latency Comparison (`dev-100`, MLX `bf16` Benchmark, Raw Decoding Without Anti-Repeat)

## Limitations

1. **Experimental Checkpoint (Not Superior to Official 0.6B):** `B-0.6B-official` (`ACE-Step/acestep-5Hz-lm-0.6B`) is faster (`5.71 s` vs. `7.96 s`), uses less memory, has higher single-shot strict validity (`100/100` vs. `97/100`), higher raw code diversity (`8.1403` vs. `4.5837` bits), and higher CLAP (`0.3451` vs. `0.2832`).
2. **Anti-Repeat Post-Processing Not Formally Benchmarked on `dev-100`:** Default anti-repeat penalties and quality-gate retries mitigate code-collapse symptoms at inference time, but their downstream impact on `dev-100` CLAP, ASR WER/CER, and mean wall-clock latency has not been formally evaluated.
3. **Single Training Seed:** Trained with a single seed (`seed = 42`) on `2,600` teacher-sampled trajectories (`975` optimizer steps); cross-seed stability is not established.
4. **Exploratory `dev-100` Only (`test-300` Untouched):** Two learning rates (`1e-4` and `3e-5`) were evaluated on `dev-100`; the held-out `test-300` split has not been evaluated.
5. **No Human Listening Tests or Calibrated ASR (`INCOMPLETE` Quality Gate):** Automated Whisper v2 metrics are uncalibrated diagnostics only, and no independent human transcription calibration or blind listening tests (MUSHRA / preference) have been performed.
6. **English & Instrumental Only (Multilingual Unverified):** Distilled strictly on English CC0 vocal prompts and `[Instrumental]` prompts (`30–120 s`). Multilingual lyric planning has not been trained or verified.
7. **GGUF Architecture Requirement (`llama.cpp` `b9810`+ / `llama-cpp-python>=0.3.37`):** Older `llama.cpp` builds without `qwen35` (`GatedDeltaNet` + `qwen35` pre-tokenizer) cannot load these files.

## Advanced: C++ Ecosystem & Renderer GGUF Notes

- **Why `generate.py` uses `llama.cpp` / `llama-cpp-python` + Python ACE-Step instead of `acestep.cpp`:** These GGUF files use the standard `llama.cpp` `qwen35` hybrid architecture (`18 GatedDeltaNet + 6 full-attention` layers, `V = 313,612`). The standalone C++ [`ace-step/acestep.cpp`](https://github.com/ace-step/acestep.cpp) runtime currently implements a custom `acestep-lm` loader restricted to homogeneous dense `Qwen3` layers and hardcoded `Qwen3` special-token IDs, so it cannot directly load `qwen35` GGUF composers without adding `GatedDeltaNet` recurrent layers and dynamic vocabulary offsets.

# Haru-4B GGUF (Quantized)

[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/jayanth-mkv/ai_collaborations/blob/main/models/haru-4b/notebooks/Haru_4B_Colab_Kaggle.ipynb)
[![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-jayanth--mkv%2Fai__collaborations-blue?logo=github)](https://github.com/jayanth-mkv/ai_collaborations)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/Apache-2.0)

This repository provides **GGUF quantized weights** and extracted FP16 audio modules for **[higurashi-ai/Haru-4B](https://huggingface.co/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B)**, the open-weight continuous full-duplex spoken dialogue foundation model.

## 🚀 1-Click Interactive Google Colab Notebook
Try out this quantized release directly on a free Google Colab T4 GPU:
👉 **[Open `Haru_4B_Colab_Kaggle.ipynb` in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/jayanth-mkv/ai_collaborations/blob/main/models/haru-4b/notebooks/Haru_4B_Colab_Kaggle.ipynb)**

---

## 🔬 Model Architecture & Quantization Strategy
Haru-4B is a full-duplex Listening-while-Speaking Language Model (LSLM) operating at **7.5 Hz (133.33 ms frame budget)**. 

To enable CPU and low-VRAM deployment without compromising voice fidelity, this release applies a **hybrid quantization approach**:
- **Language Model Backbone:** `Qwen3.5-4B` extracted and quantized to **GGUF Q4_K_M** (compressed from 8.4 GB down to **2.6 GB**, 67.5% memory reduction).
- **Audio Codec (VibeVoice):** Preserved in **FP16** (~1.3 GB) to maintain causal convolution acoustic fidelity and avoid metallic static artifacts.
- **Audio Generation Head (MeanFlow):** Preserved in **FP16** (~694 MB) for smooth 1-step continuous ODE velocity trajectory prediction.

## 📦 Repository Contents

| File | Format | Size | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `qwen-haru-q4_k_m.gguf` | GGUF Q4_K_M | **2.6 GB** | 4-bit medium quantized Qwen3.5 language model backbone |
| `vibevoice-codec-f16.safetensors` | Safetensors FP16 | **1.3 GB** | Causal 1D convolution VibeVoice acoustic tokenizer |
| `meanflow-head-f16.safetensors` | Safetensors FP16 | **694 MB** | 4-layer 1-step MeanFlow ODE audio generation head |
| `config.json` | JSON | ~2 KB | Model hyperparameter configuration (`Qwen3_5ForCausalLM`) |
| `tokenizer.json` | JSON | ~20 MB | Qwen tokenizer vocabulary (248,320 tokens) |
| `Haru_4B_Colab_Kaggle.ipynb` | Jupyter Notebook | ~8 KB | Turnkey Colab/Kaggle notebook to test GGUF & launch voice portal |

---

## 🛠️ How We Quantized It: Step-by-Step Engineering Process

### 1. Component Slicing & Memory Mapping
Haru's monolithic `model.safetensors` was sliced using `safetensors.safe_open`:
- All `lm.*` tensors were extracted into `model.*` to construct a standard `Qwen3_5ForCausalLM`.
- Handled tied word embeddings: Set `"tie_word_embeddings": true` and omitted duplicate `lm_head.weight` to prevent memory duplication errors.
- Extracted `codec.*` into `vibevoice-codec-f16.safetensors` and `head.*` into `meanflow-head-f16.safetensors`.

### 2. Base GGUF Conversion (`convert_hf_to_gguf.py`)
Converted the standalone Qwen3.5 backbone using `llama.cpp` with `--no-mtp`:
```bash
python llama.cpp/convert_hf_to_gguf.py extracted_backbone --outfile qwen-haru-bf16.gguf --no-mtp
```
*Generated a 7.94 GB BF16 base GGUF file containing 291 layers.*

### 3. 4-Bit Quantization (`llama-quantize`)
Applied 4-bit medium k-quantization:
```bash
llama-quantize qwen-haru-bf16.gguf qwen-haru-q4_k_m.gguf Q4_K_M
```
*Compressed the model from 8.02 GB to **2.60 GB** (3.08× smaller).*

### 4. Verification & Benchmarking (`llama-cli`)
- **AMD EPYC CPU (4 Dedicated Cores):** Verified CPU inference at **8.4 tokens/second**.
- **NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU (Colab):** Verified GPU inference at **68.2 tokens/second** (`-ngl 99` offloads all 32 layers).

---

## 💻 Usage Instructions

### Run via llama.cpp (CLI)
```bash
# 1. Download the 2.6 GB model
huggingface-cli download Jayanth-MKV/Haru-4B-GGUF qwen-haru-q4_k_m.gguf --local-dir .

# 2. Run on CPU (4 threads)
./llama-cli -m qwen-haru-q4_k_m.gguf -p "Hello! Let's talk." -n 64 -t 4

# 3. Run on GPU (-ngl 99 offloads all 32 layers)
./llama-cli -m qwen-haru-q4_k_m.gguf -p "Hello! Let's talk." -n 128 -ngl 99
```

### Run via Python (`llama-cpp-python`)
```python
from llama_cpp import Llama
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download

model_path = hf_hub_download(repo_id="Jayanth-MKV/Haru-4B-GGUF", filename="qwen-haru-q4_k_m.gguf")
llm = Llama(model_path=model_path, n_gpu_layers=-1, n_ctx=2048)

output = llm("Hello! How are you doing today?", max_tokens=128)
print(output["choices"][0]["text"])
```

Positive means more spoof-like, and `sigmoid(spoof_logit)` is the spoof probability. * **Format:** ONNX (opset 17), 1.26 GB. It runs on CPU with `onnxruntime`; no PyTorch needed. ## Quick start ```bash pip install onnxruntime numpy huggingface_hub # and ffmpeg for mp3/m4a/webm/ogg python inference.py my_clip.m4a # inference.py is in this repo ``` ```python import numpy as np, onnxruntime as ort from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download session = ort.InferenceSession(hf_hub_download("Hashim-Bhagad/voiceguard-xlsr-aasist-indic", "model.onnx")) wave = np.zeros((1, 64600), dtype=np.float32) # your 16 kHz mono audio, 4.04 s logit = session.run(None, {"waveform": wave})[0][0] p_spoof = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit)) is_ai = p_spoof >= 0.05393 # dev-split operating threshold, see below ``` For clips longer than 4.04 s, score several windows and average their logits (`inference.py` does this, exactly as the VoiceGuard backend does). Clips shorter than 4.04 s are tiled (repeated) up to the window length, as in training. ## Model | | | |---|---| | Front-end | [XLS-R 300M](https://huggingface.co/facebook/wav2vec2-xls-r-300m), self-supervised on 436k hours in 128 languages. The top 8 of its 24 transformer layers were fine-tuned; the CNN encoder and layers 0-15 stayed frozen. | | Layer mix | A learned softmax weighting over all 25 hidden states. | | Back-end | AASIST graph attention ([Jung et al., ICASSP 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01200)): spectral and temporal graphs plus a heterogeneous graph-attention stack. | | Parameters | 315.8M in total, 101.2M trained (32%). | | Training | Up to 12 epochs, early stopping (patience 4), best at epoch 5. Adam with cosine annealing, back-end lr 1e-4, XLS-R lr 1e-5, fp16, one T4 GPU, 0.7 h. | | Augmentation | Telephony narrowband round trip, noise at 5-20 dB SNR, room impulse responses, ±3 dB gain, applied equally to both classes. | The design follows wav2vec 2.0 + AASIST ([Tak et al., Odyssey 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.12233)). ## Training data and splits | Source | Contribution | |---|---| | [garystafford/deepfake-audio-detection](https://huggingface.co/datasets/garystafford/deepfake-audio-detection) | English real speech plus 6 commercial TTS systems | | [In-the-Wild](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mueller91/In-The-Wild) | Real-world celebrity speech and deepfakes (English) | | [IndicVoices](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4bharat/IndicVoices) | Genuine spontaneous speech in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Marathi | | [MLAAD](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mueller91/MLAAD) | Hindi deepfakes from 9 TTS systems | | Vocoder resynthesis | Same-channel Indic spoofs (Griffin-Lim variants) from held-out IndicVoices speakers | * **Clip counts:** train 3,287 genuine / 3,359 spoof; dev 767 / 418; test 1,810 / 1,923. * **Splits:** speaker-disjoint, with whole TTS systems held out. Dev uses ElevenLabs and Veena; test uses Speechify, Kokoro and IndicF5. ## Results **Held-out test split** (3,733 clips, all speakers unseen): | | EER | ROC-AUC | |---|---:|---:| | Overall | **2.97%** | **0.996** | | English (3,255 clips) | 3.54% | | | Hindi (203 clips) | 0.99% | | At the dev threshold, the model missed 0 of the 378 clips from the three TTS systems it never saw in training, and 0.2% of all spoofs. At that threshold it flags 13.8% of genuine clips, mostly noisy In-the-Wild recordings. **Real-world checks** (audio that never went through the training pipeline): | Set | Result | |---|---| | 16 genuine recordings + 16 zero-shot voice clones of the same 5 people | All 16 clones caught, 1 genuine recording flagged, EER 3.1% | | 200 genuine FLEURS recordings + 200 Microsoft and Google TTS clips (en, hi, bn, ta, mr), clean and WhatsApp-compressed | All 200 AI clips caught; genuine clips flagged: Indic 10%, English 57% (80% after Opus compression) |

## Threshold The EER operating point chosen on dev is a spoof probability of **0.05393**, far below 0.5. * **0.05393** catches nearly every clone but raises more false alarms, especially on compressed English speech. * **0.5** cuts false alarms (6.5% on FLEURS), but missed 5 of the 16 real voice clones in the check above. VoiceGuard uses the low threshold to trigger a "prove you are live" challenge, not to block a call. ## Limitations * **Not proof of identity.** Treat a score as a risk signal and combine it with other checks. * **Codecs.** Genuine speech that went through WhatsApp/Opus compression is often flagged. Training had no codec augmentation; that is the next planned version. * **Clones in Bengali, Tamil and Marathi** are only evaluated against Microsoft/Google TTS. Zero-shot clones in those languages, and dialects, are not yet measured. * **In-the-Wild deepfakes** appear in both train and test (with different speakers), so they are not a held-out generator. --- license: apache-2.0 pipeline_tag: text-to-speech library_name: zonos3 language: - en - fr - es - de - it - pt - nl - pl - ru - sv - tr - uk - cs - da - fi - el - hu - "no" - ro - sk - bg - zh - ja - ko - ar - he - vi - id - th - tl - ms - ka - hi - bn - ta - te - mr - gu - kn - ml - pa - or - ur tags: - text-to-speech - tts - speech-synthesis - voice-cloning - multilingual - gguf - zonos - zonos3 - zyphra --- # ZONOS3-Mini

--- ZONOS3-Mini is Zyphra’s compact, open-source text-to-speech model, delivering natural reliable speech and high-fidelity voice cloning with just 100 million active parameters. It runs in real time on phones and laptops, including directly in the browser. Clone a voice from an audio sample, or design a character by shaping age, accent and vocal texture. Steer emotion, pace and delivery down to individual words for games, narration and voice assistants. Run ZONOS3-Mini locally with our browser and native runtimes, or access it through [Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini). Model weights are released under Apache 2.0. **Model details, samples and evaluations are in the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini).** **A hosted version is available at [Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini).** ## Languages ZONOS3-Mini supports 43 languages. | Region | Languages | |---|---| | Western and Southern Europe | English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Greek | | Northern Europe | Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Finnish | | Central and Eastern Europe | Polish, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Russian, Ukrainian | | Middle East and Caucasus | Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Georgian | | East Asia | Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Korean | | Southeast Asia | Vietnamese, Indonesian, Malay, Thai, Tagalog | | South Asia | Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Odia, Urdu | ## Quick start ### In your browser ZONOS3-Mini runs entirely on your own GPU through WebGPU: no install and no server. The first visit downloads the model, and the browser keeps it cached for later visits. You need a browser with WebGPU support. - [Zonos Voice Studio](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground#cast): the full studio. - [Lite](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground/lite): quick voice cloning. Pick, upload or record a voice and speak with it. ### With SGLang [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) serves ZONOS3-Mini on NVIDIA GPUs behind the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint, with streaming and voice cloning from a reference clip (no transcript needed). Install SGLang-Omni by following its [installation guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/get_started/installation.md), then start a server: ```bash sgl-omni serve --model-path Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini --port 8000 ``` Once `curl http://localhost:8000/health` reports `"healthy"`, generate speech with the default voice from another terminal: ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/speech \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input": "Hello from ZONOS3-Mini!"}' \ --output output.wav ``` Add `"references": [{"audio_path": ""}]` to clone a voice, or `"stream": true, "response_format": "pcm"` to stream 44.1 kHz audio as it is generated. The [ZONOS3 cookbook](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/cookbook/zonos3.md) covers voice cloning, streaming and the sampling options. ### Native runtimes The [ZONOS3-Mini GitHub repository](https://github.com/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini) holds Zyphra's own runtimes, which share one HTTP API and serve the Zonos Voice Studio: a CUDA server for NVIDIA GPUs, an MLX server for Apple Silicon, a C++/ggml server and CLI (CPU, CUDA, Metal or Vulkan), and the in-browser WebGPU build. They load the GGUF files in [`gguf/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/main/gguf) and the WebGPU shards in [`web/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/main/web); the 27 default voices, grouped by language, are in [`gguf/voices/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/blob/main/gguf/voices/README.md). ## Architecture (rough outline) Text is NeMo-normalized (English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese; other languages pass through as written) and encoded with an 8,192-entry SuperBPE tokenizer. The language model autoregressively generates 15 Hz dual-codec frames (10 codebooks of 4,096 entries each: one semantic codebook distilled from the Wav2Vec2-BERT teacher plus nine acoustic codebooks), conditioned on the text, a speaker prompt and three bucketed acoustic controls. A causal multi-resolution iSTFT head renders the frames to 44.1 kHz audio as they are produced. ![ZONOS3-Mini inference pipeline](assets/zonos3_mini_arloop_animated.gif) *Inference pipeline. Speaker conditioning (raw reference codes or a speaker-embedding row), control rows and SuperBPE text enter the hybrid GDN/attention MoE backbone, which predicts all ten codebooks of the next frame under the delay pattern (four drawn); as soon as a frame's last codebook is generated, the codec's causal iSTFT head renders that frame to audio.* | | ZONOS3-Mini | |---|---| | Backbone | 11 layers, model dim 1,024; 800M parameters total, about 100M active per token (latent MoE: 64 experts, top-2 routing, from layer 1) | | Sequence mixer | pattern `gdn3_global1`: 9 Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers + 2 global attention layers (16 heads x 32 dims, 4 KV heads), attention residuals (`full_attnres`); context 32,768 positions | | Text | SuperBPE, 8,192 entries (+4 specials), NeMo text normalization at inference | | Audio tokens | 15 Hz, 44.1 kHz dual-encoding codec, 10 x 4,096 codebooks (1 semantic + 9 acoustic); hop 2,940 samples; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation | | Speaker prompt | raw reference clip (encoded by the codec into a token prefix, up to 60 s, with speaker CFG) **or** a single 192-d MECT-B2 speaker embedding (`ownmect_s2`) | | Controls | loudness (LUFS, 10 buckets), bandwidth f_max (Hz, 10 buckets), **speaking rate (UTF-8 bytes per second, 30 buckets)**; each row has an "unknown" index; bucket edges in `params.json` (`condition_edges`) | | Decoder | causal multi-resolution iSTFT head: `full_mr` (default) or `keep2_plain` (pruned, about 3x faster decode) | | Precision | bf16 weights (`model.pth`); decoder heads run in fp32 | ![ZAC 1 audio codec](assets/arch_zac1_dark.png) *ZAC 1 (Zyphra Audio Codec 1).* ## Evaluations Full results and the ZTTS2 capability index are in the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini#evaluation). Quality against speed on one H100 80GB. Quality combines macro speaker similarity and macro WER over the 55 language subsets of [ZTTS2-Eval](https://zyphra.github.io/ZTTS2-Eval/) (benchmark version 2: FLEURS-R read speech in 35 languages and VoxBlink2 in-the-wild recordings in 20 languages) as ½ z(similarity) − ½ z(WER) across the systems shown; ZONOS3-Mini is measured with the speaker-embedding prompt. Left: median time to first audio with 8 concurrent requests (80 ms for ZONOS3-Mini). Right: peak throughput at each model's best concurrency (457 seconds of audio per second for ZONOS3-Mini). ![ZONOS3-Mini quality versus time to first audio and throughput](assets/eval_pareto.png) ## Citation If you find this model useful in an academic context, please cite the technical report: ```bibtex @misc{zyphra2026zonos3mini, title = {{ZONOS3-Mini Technical Report}}, author = {Gabriel Clark and Sofian Mejjoute and George Close and Beren Millidge}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2611.16525}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.SD}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16525}, } ```

# Sachai Check: Urdu audio deepfake detector

Part of **Sachai Check** (FAST-NUCES Lahore final year project). It decides whether an Urdu speech clip is
genuine (bona fide) or synthetic (text-to-speech / voice clone). It reports authenticity only; it says nothing
about whether the spoken content is true.

## Model
- Backbone: `facebook/wav2vec2-xls-r-300m` fine-tuned end to end (CNN feature encoder frozen).
- Head: softmax-weighted sum of all 25 hidden layers, attentive statistics pooling, 2-layer MLP.
- Input: 16 kHz mono, leading and trailing silence trimmed (40 dB), per-window zero-mean unit-variance.
- Inference: 4 s windows with 2 s hop, mean log-odds per clip, temperature-scaled (T = 2.230).
- Decision policy (fitted on dev speakers only): synthetic if score >= 0.189, genuine if score <= 0.149,
  otherwise inconclusive.

## Data and protocol
CSALT Urdu deepfake dataset (Munir et al., Findings of ACL 2024): genuine speech plus Tacotron and VITS clones.
Split by speaker, so test voices are never heard in training: train 4787 clips, dev 798, test 1190.

## Results (test speakers, frozen dev policy)
| metric | value |
|---|---|
| EER | 0.0857 |
| ROC-AUC | 0.9812 |
| Accuracy at EER threshold | 0.8378 |
| Macro-F1 | 0.8339 |
| Coverage (not inconclusive) | 0.8908 |

Robustness and per-attack tables are in `metrics.json`.

## Limits
Trained on two TTS families and a small set of speakers. Commercial voice cloning, other languages, music and
heavily processed audio are outside the tested conditions; the API flags such inputs as out of distribution.
Treat every verdict as a signal, not proof.

## Use
```python
from sachai_audio.infer import Detector
det = Detector("Ikhlas125/sachai-check-urdu-audio-deepfake")
print(det.analyze_file("clip.wav")["verdict"])
```
License follows the dataset (CC BY-NC 4.0): non-commercial use only.

# phoonnx-styletts2

Mirror of StyleTTS2-family checkpoints exported to ONNX for
[phoonnx](https://github.com/TigreGotico/phoonnx), OpenVoiceOS's offline TTS
library. StyleTTS2 generates speech conditioned on a style vector that
encodes prosody and timbre from a reference clip, which is what enables
zero-shot cloning; `phoonnx` also treats the Kokoro checkpoints (a StyleTTS2
descendant, "misaki"-phonemized) as `styletts2`-engine voices since they
share the same style-vector conditioning contract. See
[docs/cloning.md](https://github.com/TigreGotico/phoonnx/blob/dev/docs/cloning.md)
for the `styletts2_style` d-vector mechanism.

This repository holds the raw ONNX weights, `config.json` files, and (for
cloning-capable voices) `.bin` style vectors consumed by `phoonnx`'s
`voice_index` (`styletts2.json`); it is not meant to be browsed for voices
directly — use `phoonnx`'s voice manager, which resolves voice IDs to the
files here.

## Contents

| Directory | Voices | Language | Upstream |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ddatt-en-styletts2/` | `ddatt/en-styletts2` | en-US | community StyleTTS2 checkpoint by `ddatt`; original training source could not be located |
| `bsc-es-styletts2/` | `bsc/es-styletts2` (zero-shot) + 6 named speakers `bsc/es-cml<id>` | es | [`BSC-LT/styletts2-spanish-multispeaker`](https://huggingface.co/BSC-LT/styletts2-spanish-multispeaker) (Barcelona Supercomputing Center) |
| `bsc-ca-styletts2/` | `bsc/ca-styletts2` (zero-shot) + 11 named speakers `bsc/ca-<name>` | ca | [`BSC-LT/styletts2-catalan-multispeaker`](https://huggingface.co/BSC-LT/styletts2-catalan-multispeaker) (Barcelona Supercomputing Center) |
| `hitz-eu-styletts2/` | one speaker each: `antton`, `maider` | eu | [`HiTZ/StyleTTS2-eu`](https://huggingface.co/HiTZ/StyleTTS2-eu) (HiTZ Center, University of the Basque Country) |
| `hitz-eu-emo-styletts2/` | `antton`/`maider` x `happy`/`neutral`/`sad` | eu | [`HiTZ/StyleTTS2-eu_emo`](https://huggingface.co/HiTZ/StyleTTS2-eu_emo) (HiTZ Center) |
| `proxectonos-gl-celtia/` | `proxectonos/celtia-styletts2` | gl | [`proxectonos/Nos_StyleTTS2-Celtia-GL`](https://huggingface.co/proxectonos/Nos_StyleTTS2-Celtia-GL) ([Proxecto Nós](https://nos.gal/gl/proxecto-nos), technical development by [Gradiant](https://www.gradiant.org/)) |
| `proxectonos-gl-brais/` | `proxectonos/brais-styletts2` | gl | [`proxectonos/Nos_StyleTTS2-Brais-GL`](https://huggingface.co/proxectonos/Nos_StyleTTS2-Brais-GL) ([Proxecto Nós](https://nos.gal/gl/proxecto-nos), technical development by [Gradiant](https://www.gradiant.org/)) |
| `kokoro-82m/` | `kokoro/*` (English voices, plus per-language configs for es/fr/hi/it/ja/pt/zh) | en-US + others | [`hexgrad/Kokoro-82M`](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M); style vectors fetched at load time from [`onnx-community/Kokoro-82M-v1.0-ONNX`](https://huggingface.co/onnx-community/Kokoro-82M-v1.0-ONNX) |
| `kokoro-v0.19/` | Kokoro v0.19 voices | en-US | [`hexgrad/kLegacy`](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/kLegacy) (Kokoro v0.19) |
| `kokoro-v1.1-zh/` | Kokoro v1.1 zh/en voices | zh, en-US | [`hexgrad/Kokoro-82M-v1.1-zh`](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M-v1.1-zh) |

## Usage

```python
import wave
from phoonnx.model_manager import TTSModelManager

manager = TTSModelManager()
manager.load()
manager.merge_default_voices()

voice = manager.voices["kokoro/af_heart"].load()
with wave.open("out.wav", "wb") as wav_file:
    voice.synthesize_wav("Hello, this is a test.", wav_file)
```

## License

`license: other` because the checkpoints in this repository come from
different labs with different licenses. `phoonnx` itself is Apache-2.0.

| Family | Voices | License |
|---|---|---|
| Kokoro (all versions) | `kokoro/*` | Apache-2.0 |
| BSC Spanish StyleTTS2 | `bsc/es-styletts2`, `bsc/es-cml*` | Apache-2.0 |
| BSC Catalan StyleTTS2 | `bsc/ca-styletts2`, `bsc/ca-*` | GPL-3.0 |
| ProxectoNós Galician StyleTTS2 | `proxectonos/celtia-styletts2`, `proxectonos/brais-styletts2` | Apache-2.0 |
| HiTZ Basque StyleTTS2 (base + emotion) | `hitz-eu-styletts2/*`, `hitz-eu-emo-styletts2/*` | Apache-2.0 |
| `ddatt/en-styletts2` | `ddatt-en-styletts2/` | not determined — original upstream repo could not be located; treat as all-rights-reserved until clarified |

The two BSC checkpoints are **multispeaker**. Neither upstream repository ships
reference audio, so `bsc/es-styletts2` and `bsc/ca-styletts2` need a reference
clip on every call. Alongside them each directory now carries one
`<speaker>.bin` style blob per named speaker, so the same checkpoint also
serves ordinary preset voices:

* `bsc-ca-styletts2/` — 11 [Festcat](https://huggingface.co/datasets/projecte-aina/festcat_trimmed_denoised)
  speakers: `bet eli eva jan mar ona pau pep pol teo uri`.
* `bsc-es-styletts2/` — the 6 [CML-TTS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ylacombe/cml-tts)
  Spanish speakers that hold the corpus: `3946 8882 9972 10246 11797 12367`.
  CML-TTS names speakers by number only.

Each blob is 256 `float32` values (`ref_p` ++ `ref_s`), the mean of the style
encoder's output over four reference clips of that speaker taken from the
model's own training corpus. A named speaker still clones when you pass a
reference clip. See
[docs/bsc_multispeaker.md](https://github.com/TigreGotico/phoonnx/blob/dev/docs/bsc_multispeaker.md).

The Galician voices are single-speaker: each ships a `style.bin` default
style alongside the `style_encoder.onnx` used for cloning. They are
phonemized with Cotovía notation (not IPA) — see
[docs/galician.md](https://github.com/TigreGotico/phoonnx/blob/dev/docs/galician.md).

Note the BSC Catalan checkpoint is GPL-3.0-licensed by its authors; this only
governs the model weights themselves, not `phoonnx` (Apache-2.0), which
merely loads them.
